senses.gloss: Forming a united whole; working or fitting together well.
examples: The new coach turned them into a *cohesive* team.
Your essay needs a more *cohesive* structure.
The neighborhood has always been close and *cohesive*.

senses.gloss: Wound into rings or a spiral.
examples: A *coiled* rattlesnake lay under the rock.
The garden hose was neatly *coiled* by the door.
She wore her hair in a tight *coiled* bun.

senses.gloss: Working only when you put coins into it.
examples: The building has *coin-operated* washers in the basement.
All the parking meters here are *coin-operated*.
We found an old *coin-operated* arcade game at the diner.

senses.gloss: Happening by chance, not because it was planned.
examples: Any resemblance to real people is purely *coincidental*.
It was a *coincidental* meeting at the airport.
I don't think the timing was *coincidental*.

contrast: To say you feel cold, English uses the person as subject: *I'm cold* = мне холодно, not «я холодный». *It's cold* is about the weather or a room. *A cold* is a noun (простуда): *I have a cold*.

senses.gloss: Having a low temperature.
examples: It's *cold* outside, so take a jacket.
January is usually the *coldest* month in Chicago.
Can I get a *cold* glass of water?

senses.gloss: Feeling that your body is not warm enough.
examples: I'm *cold* — can you close the window?
The kids were wet and *cold* after the game.

senses.gloss: Unfriendly and showing no warm feelings.
examples: She gave me a *cold* look and walked away.
His voice got *colder* when I mentioned the money.

senses.gloss: Unconscious, especially after being hit; used in *out cold*.
examples: The boxer was out *cold* for a full minute.
He hit his head on the ice and was knocked out *cold*.

contrast: Russian *хладнокровный* is usually praise (calm under pressure); English *cold-blooded* is always negative about people — it means cruel. For calm, say *cool-headed* or *calm*.

senses.gloss: Cruel and showing no emotion.
examples: It was a *cold-blooded* murder.
The jury saw him as a *cold-blooded* killer.
That was the most *cold-blooded* thing I've ever seen.

senses.gloss: Having a body temperature that changes with the surroundings, like reptiles and fish.
examples: Snakes are *cold-blooded*, so they lie in the sun.
*Cold-blooded* animals slow down in cold weather.

senses.gloss: Crying a lot because of stomach pain; used mostly about babies.
examples: Our *colicky* baby cried every night for three months.
She gets *colicky* after feedings.
Some babies are just more *colicky* than others.

senses.gloss: Done by people working together.
examples: The album was a *collaborative* project between two bands.
We want a more *collaborative* office culture.
The whole process was very *collaborative*.

senses.gloss: Able to be folded into a smaller shape.
examples: We keep two *collapsible* chairs in the trunk.
The stroller is *collapsible*, so it fits in the closet.
Take a *collapsible* water bottle on the hike.

contrast: The noun *collateral* is залог — property you promise to a lender: *He used his house as collateral*. The adjective appears mainly in *collateral damage*.

senses.gloss: Happening as an extra, unintended result of something.
examples: The airstrike caused heavy *collateral* damage.
Innocent people became *collateral* victims of the feud.
Budget cuts had *collateral* effects on local schools.

position: both — sense 2 before a noun only

senses.gloss: Calm and in control of your feelings.
examples: She stayed calm and *collected* during the interview.
He seemed more *collected* after a glass of water.

senses.gloss: Brought together in one book or set.
examples: I bought the *collected* works of Mark Twain.
Her *collected* essays came out last fall.

contrast: Also a noun: *He sells collectibles online*. The spelling *collectable* exists but *collectible* is the usual American form.

senses.gloss: Worth collecting because people value it.
examples: Old baseball cards are highly *collectible*.
The store sells *collectible* coins and stamps.
First editions are the most *collectible* copies.

contrast: Russian *коллектив* (the staff, the team) is not English *collective*: say *the staff*, *the team*, *my coworkers*. The noun *a collective* is a group that owns or runs something together, like a farm or an art space.

senses.gloss: Shared or done by all the members of a group.
examples: It was a *collective* decision.
We breathed a *collective* sigh of relief.
The union won the right to *collective* bargaining.

senses.gloss: Friendly and respectful between people who work together.
senses.ru: дружеский, основанный на взаимном уважении коллег
examples: The department has a very *collegial* atmosphere.
Despite their disagreements, the debate stayed *collegial*.
The new manager is more *collegial* than the last one.

contrast: A false friend: *collegiate* is about colleges and college students, not *коллегиальный* (decided together) — that is *collective* or *joint*.

senses.gloss: Relating to a college or to college students.
examples: She won three *collegiate* swimming titles.
*Collegiate* athletes can now earn money from sponsorships.
He kept his *collegiate* dictionary on the desk.

senses.gloss: Used in informal conversation rather than formal writing.
examples: "Gonna" is a *colloquial* form of "going to."
Her English sounds natural and *colloquial*.
The translation is more *colloquial* than the original.

contrast: The country is spelled *Colombia*, with two *o*s; *Columbia* is a US river, a university and the District of Columbia. It is also a noun: *a Colombian* (колумбиец).

senses.gloss: From or relating to Colombia.
examples: We only buy *Colombian* coffee.
Her mother is *Colombian* and her father is Mexican.
The restaurant serves traditional *Colombian* food.

senses.gloss: Relating to a colony or to a country's rule over colonies.
examples: The country won independence from *colonial* rule in 1960.
Many borders in Africa are *colonial* inventions.

senses.gloss: In the US, from the time before independence, or built in that style.
senses.ru: колониальный (о периоде до 1776 г. и стиле)
examples: They live in a white *colonial* house with black shutters.
Williamsburg recreates *colonial* life in Virginia.

senses.gloss: Unable to see the difference between certain colors.
examples: My dad is *color-blind* and can't tell red from green.
*Color-blind* drivers learn the order of the traffic lights.

senses.gloss: Treating people the same regardless of race.
examples: The company claims its hiring is *color-blind*.
Critics say a *color-blind* approach ignores real inequality.

senses.gloss: Relating to the colon and rectum.
examples: Doctors recommend *colorectal* cancer screening after 45.
She was referred to a *colorectal* surgeon.
Diet can affect *colorectal* health.

contrast: About people, *colored* is dated and offensive in the US; say *people of color* or name the group. For things it is neutral, often with an adverb or color word: *brightly colored*, *cream-colored*.

senses.gloss: Having a color, or a particular color, rather than being white, black or clear.
examples: The kids drew with *colored* pencils.
The birds were brightly *colored*.
She wore a cream-*colored* dress to the wedding.

senses.gloss: Having many bright colors.
examples: The market was full of *colorful* fruit.
Her kitchen is much more *colorful* than mine.

senses.gloss: Interesting, lively and a little unusual.
examples: My grandfather was a *colorful* character.
The town has a long and *colorful* history.

senses.gloss: Of language, rude or full of swearing; a polite way to say it.
examples: The coach used some *colorful* language after the loss.
His description of his boss was *colorful*, to say the least.

senses.gloss: Having no color.
examples: Water is a *colorless* liquid.
Carbon monoxide is *colorless* and has no smell.

senses.gloss: Dull and not interesting.
examples: He gave a *colorless* speech that nobody remembers.
The sequel was even more *colorless* than the first movie.

contrast: An extreme adjective: use *absolutely* or *truly*, not *very* — ✗ *very colossal* → *a truly colossal mistake*. In American speech it is often about mistakes and failures: *a colossal waste of time*.

senses.gloss: Extremely large.
examples: The project was a *colossal* waste of money.
A *colossal* statue stands at the entrance.
The cost of the repairs was *colossal*.

senses.gloss: In a coma.
examples: The patient remained *comatose* for two weeks.
Doctors spoke to his family at the *comatose* man's bedside.

senses.gloss: Very tired, sleepy or inactive; used humorously.
examples: After Thanksgiving dinner, everyone was *comatose* on the couch.
The class looked *comatose* by the end of the lecture.

senses.gloss: Trained and equipped to fight.
examples: The general said the troops were *combat-ready*.
The Navy needs more *combat-ready* ships.
It takes months to make a new unit *combat-ready*.

senses.gloss: Ready and eager to argue or fight.
examples: The senator was *combative* with reporters.
He gave a *combative* interview on cable news.
The second debate was even more *combative* than the first.

position: attributive only — also right after a noun in *…combined* (вместе взятые)

senses.gloss: Added or joined together.
examples: Their *combined* income is about $150,000.
It took a *combined* effort to move the piano.
He earns more than the rest of us *combined*.

senses.gloss: Able to catch fire and burn easily.
examples: Keep *combustible* materials away from the stove.
Dry leaves are highly *combustible*.

senses.gloss: Likely to become angry or violent quickly.
examples: The protest created a *combustible* situation.
The mix of anger and alcohol made the crowd more *combustible*.

takes: *with* + noun or *-ing* (at ease with); *doing* or *about* in speech
contrast: Say it in three syllables: KUHMF-tur-buhl, not com-FOR-ta-ble. The person is the subject for how you feel: *I'm comfortable* = мне удобно; *The chair is comfortable* = стул удобный.

senses.gloss: Pleasant to wear, sit on or be in; giving physical comfort.
examples: These are the most *comfortable* shoes I own.
The hotel beds were really *comfortable*.

senses.gloss: Relaxed and not worried or embarrassed.
examples: Make yourself *comfortable* while I get the coffee.
I'm not *comfortable* with the idea of lying to her.
She felt more *comfortable* speaking English after a year.

senses.gloss: Having enough money to live well.
examples: They live a *comfortable* life in the suburbs.
His parents are pretty *comfortable* financially.

senses.gloss: Of a lead or win, large enough to be safe.
examples: The Yankees had a *comfortable* lead in the ninth.
She won by a *comfortable* margin.

contrast: *Comforting* words make you feel less sad or worried; a *comfortable* chair is pleasant to sit in. ✗ *a comforting sofa* → *a comfortable sofa*.

senses.gloss: Making you feel less worried, sad or afraid.
examples: Thanks for the *comforting* words.
It's *comforting* to know you're nearby.
Nothing is more *comforting* than a bowl of chicken soup.

senses.gloss: Comfortable; an informal word.
examples: I changed into something *comfy* after work.
This is the *comfiest* couch in the house.
Are you *comfy* back there?

position: attributive only — after a verb use *comical* or *funny*
contrast: *Comic* mostly means "of comedy" and goes before a noun: *a comic actor*. *Comical* means funny, often unintentionally, and goes in both positions: *The situation was comical*. The noun *a comic* is a comedian or a comic book.

senses.gloss: Relating to comedy.
examples: He's best known for his *comic* roles.
The novel is a *comic* look at small-town life.

senses.gloss: Meant to make people laugh.
examples: The sidekick provides some *comic* relief.
She has perfect *comic* timing.

senses.gloss: Funny, often in a strange or silly way.
examples: The dog looked *comical* in its tiny sweater.
His attempts to dance were almost *comical*.
It was the most *comical* wedding speech I've ever heard.

contrast: Only before a noun and usually after *the*: *in the coming days*. *Upcoming* means the same and is more common for events: *the upcoming election*.

senses.gloss: Happening soon; in the near future.
examples: We'll know more in the *coming* weeks.
Prices are expected to rise in the *coming* year.
The team is preparing for the *coming* season.

position: both — senses 2 and 3 usually before a noun

senses.gloss: Having authority and making people respect and obey you.
examples: She has a *commanding* presence on stage.
His voice was calm but *commanding*.

senses.gloss: Of a lead or position, strong and likely to win; of a view, seen from a high place.
examples: The Democrats hold a *commanding* lead in the polls.
The house has a *commanding* view of the bay.

senses.gloss: In charge of a military unit.
examples: Report to your *commanding* officer.
The *commanding* general visited the base.

senses.gloss: Made or done to remember a person or event.
examples: The Mint released a *commemorative* coin.
Visitors received a *commemorative* program.
A *commemorative* plaque marks the spot.

senses.gloss: Deserving praise.
examples: Her honesty is *commendable*.
The volunteers did a *commendable* job.
What he did was even more *commendable* given his age.

position: both — often right after a noun with *with*: *salary commensurate with experience*

senses.gloss: Matching something in size, amount or level; formal.
examples: Salary is *commensurate* with experience.
The punishment should be *commensurate* with the crime.
She wants a *commensurate* increase in responsibility.

comparison: more/most — *more commercial*; not gradable in sense 1
contrast: The noun *a commercial* is a TV or radio ad (рекламный ролик). A *commercial* flight is a passenger flight on an airline, not a business trip.

senses.gloss: Relating to business and buying and selling.
examples: The building has *commercial* space on the ground floor.
He's a *commercial* airline pilot.

senses.gloss: Made to earn money or be popular rather than for art or quality.
examples: Her new album is more *commercial* than her early work.
The movie was a huge *commercial* success.

senses.gloss: Strong or good enough to be used in a business, not just at home.
examples: We put a *commercial-grade* stove in the new kitchen.
The carpet in the lobby is *commercial-grade*.
They sell *commercial-grade* equipment to gyms.

senses.gloss: Changed so that making money matters more than anything else.
examples: Christmas has become way too *commercialized*.
College sports are more *commercialized* than ever.
Some people avoid *commercialized* tourist spots.

senses.gloss: Of a military officer, holding an official rank such as lieutenant or higher.
examples: She became a *commissioned* officer after West Point.
Only *commissioned* officers may attend the briefing.

senses.gloss: Made or done because someone officially asked and paid for it.
examples: The museum displayed a *commissioned* portrait of the mayor.
The orchestra premiered a newly *commissioned* piece.

contrast: *To* here is a preposition, so it takes *-ing*: ✗ *committed to improve* → *committed to improving*.

senses.gloss: Willing to give time and energy to a job, cause or activity.
examples: We're *committed* to reducing waste.
She's one of the most *committed* teachers in the school.
The company needs *committed* volunteers.

senses.gloss: In a serious, long-term romantic relationship.
examples: They've been in a *committed* relationship for years.
He isn't ready to be *committed* to anyone.

comparison: -er/-est or more/most — *more common*, *most common*; *commoner*, *commonest* are less usual
takes: *to* + noun (shared by); *for* + noun + *to*-infinitive (*It's common for kids to…*)
contrast: Russian *общий* is wider: *the total cost* (not *common cost*), *general knowledge* (not *common knowledge*, which means "something everybody knows"). *Common sense* is a noun — здравый смысл.

senses.gloss: Happening often or existing in large numbers.
examples: Smith is the *most common* last name in the US.
It's *common* for kids to be afraid of the dark.
Back pain is becoming more *common* among office workers.

senses.gloss: Shared by two or more people or groups.
examples: We have a *common* interest in jazz.
This problem is *common* to all big cities.

senses.gloss: Ordinary; not special or of high rank.
examples: There's no cure for the *common* cold.
He talks like a *common* working man.

ru: гражданский (о браке без регистрации); основанный на общем праве
contrast: A false friend: Russian *гражданский брак* in everyday speech means living together without registering — that is *common-law marriage*. English *civil marriage* is a registered marriage without a religious ceremony.

senses.gloss: Of a husband, wife or marriage, treated as married because the couple has lived together for a long time.
examples: She's been his *common-law* wife for ten years.
Only a few states still recognize *common-law* marriage.

senses.gloss: Based on law made by past court decisions rather than written statutes.
examples: The lawyer made a *common-law* argument.
Fraud is also a *common-law* offense.

senses.gloss: Happening or seen so often that it is no longer unusual.
examples: Working from home is now *commonplace*.
Electric cars are becoming more *commonplace*.
It's a *commonplace* problem in small businesses.

ru: здравый, разумный, основанный на здравом смысле
contrast: Before a noun it is written as one word: *a commonsense solution*. After a verb, use the two-word noun: *It's just common sense*.

senses.gloss: Based on practical good judgment.
examples: We need a *commonsense* approach to gun safety.
She offered some *commonsense* advice.
The bill includes a few *commonsense* reforms.

senses.gloss: Showing practical good judgment.
examples: Her answer was simple and *commonsensical*.
He's a *commonsensical* guy who doesn't panic.
The second plan seems more *commonsensical*.

contrast: Not Russian *коммунальный*: *коммунальные услуги* are *utilities*, and *коммунальная квартира* is a *shared apartment*. English *communal* means shared by a group: *a communal kitchen*.

senses.gloss: Shared by a group of people.
examples: The dorm has a *communal* kitchen on each floor.
Dinner is served at long *communal* tables.
In the old days, the well was *communal*.

senses.gloss: Of a disease, able to pass from one person to another.
examples: Measles is a highly *communicable* disease.
The CDC tracks *communicable* diseases nationwide.
Is the infection *communicable*?

contrast: For a person who loves meeting people, English says *outgoing* or *sociable*; *communicative* means willing to talk and share information: *He isn't very communicative about his plans*.

senses.gloss: Willing to talk and give information.
examples: Teenagers aren't always very *communicative*.
The new manager is much more *communicative* than the last one.

senses.gloss: Relating to communication.
examples: The course focuses on *communicative* skills.
Many teachers use a *communicative* approach to language learning.

contrast: Also a noun: *a communist* (коммунист). Written with a capital C for a specific party: *the Communist Party*.

senses.gloss: Relating to communism or a communist party.
examples: Cuba still has a *communist* government.
Her grandparents left a *communist* country in the 1970s.
Was East Germany *communist*?

contrast: The adjective is often stressed on the second syllable (kuhm-PAKT), though KAHM-pakt is also heard; the noun *a compact* (a small car, a powder case, an agreement) is always KAHM-pakt.

senses.gloss: Small and using space efficiently.
examples: We rented a *compact* car to save on gas.
The new model is lighter and more *compact*.
Their apartment is *compact* but comfortable.

senses.gloss: Pressed closely together; dense.
examples: The soil was too *compact* for the roots to grow.
He has a short, *compact* build, like a wrestler.

senses.gloss: Friendly and pleasant to be with.
examples: We sat in *companionable* silence by the fire.
Her dog is gentle and *companionable*.
The trip made them more *companionable* than before.

contrast: The stress moves to the first syllable: KAHM-pur-uh-buhl, not kuhm-PAIR-uh-buhl as in *compare*, though the second is also heard.

senses.gloss: Similar in size, amount or quality, so that it makes sense to compare them.
examples: Rents here are *comparable* to Boston's.
She found a job at a *comparable* salary.
The two studies aren't directly *comparable*.

senses.gloss: Involving the comparison of two or more things.
examples: She teaches *comparative* literature.
The report is a *comparative* study of US and Canadian schools.
"Bigger" is the *comparative* form of "big."

senses.gloss: Measured by comparing with something else.
examples: After the city, we enjoyed the *comparative* quiet of the farm.
He passed the test with *comparative* ease.

senses.gloss: Divided into separate sections or kept strictly apart.
examples: The bag has a *compartmentalized* interior.
Information in the agency is highly *compartmentalized*.
He keeps his work and family life very *compartmentalized*.

senses.gloss: Feeling or showing sympathy and a wish to help people who suffer.
examples: She's a kind and *compassionate* nurse.
The judge was *compassionate* toward the young defendant.
We need a more *compassionate* immigration system.

senses.gloss: Able to work with another device, program or system.
examples: Is this charger *compatible* with my phone?
The software isn't *compatible* with older Macs.

senses.gloss: Able to live or work together happily.
examples: We're just not *compatible* as roommates.
The app matches you with the most *compatible* people nearby.

senses.gloss: Able to exist together without conflict.
examples: Is economic growth *compatible* with protecting the environment?
His actions aren't *compatible* with his promises.

senses.gloss: Strong enough to make you believe or act.
examples: The prosecution presented *compelling* evidence.
Give me one *compelling* reason to stay.

senses.gloss: So interesting that you want to keep watching, reading or listening.
examples: It's the most *compelling* documentary I've seen this year.
The characters are *compelling* from the first page.

takes: *at* or *in* + noun or *-ing*; *to*-infinitive (legal: *competent to stand trial*)
contrast: English *competent* often means only "good enough": *a competent performance* is solid, not brilliant. Russian *компетентный* sounds like higher praise — for that, say *highly skilled* or *expert*.

senses.gloss: Having enough skill or knowledge to do something well.
examples: We need a *competent* lawyer.
She's very *competent* at managing people.
He's more *competent* than his résumé suggests.

senses.gloss: Satisfactory but not excellent.
examples: The band gave a *competent* but boring show.
His Spanish is *competent*, not fluent.

senses.gloss: Legally able to make decisions or take part in a trial.
examples: The judge ruled that he was *competent* to stand trial.
A doctor must confirm the patient is mentally *competent*.

senses.gloss: Involving competition, where people try to win or be better than others.
examples: She played *competitive* tennis in college.
Getting into medical school is extremely *competitive*.

senses.gloss: Of a person, wanting very much to win or be the best.
examples: My brother is way too *competitive* at board games.
She's the most *competitive* person on the team.

senses.gloss: Of prices, pay or products, as good as or better than others.
examples: We offer *competitive* salaries and good benefits.
Their prices are more *competitive* than the big chains'.

senses.gloss: So pleased with how things are that you stop trying or stop seeing danger.
examples: We can't get *complacent* just because we're winning.
People have grown *complacent* about wearing seat belts.
Success made the company more *complacent*.

contrast: *Complementary* (with *e*) means completing each other; *complimentary* (with *i*) means praising or free. They sound exactly the same: *complementary colors*, *complimentary drinks*.

senses.gloss: Different but going well together, each adding what the other lacks.
examples: The two partners have *complementary* skills.
Blue and orange are *complementary* colors.
The wine is *complementary* to the cheese.

senses.gloss: Of medicine, used together with standard medical treatment.
examples: The hospital offers *complementary* therapies like acupuncture.
Yoga is often used as a *complementary* treatment.

senses.gloss: Following rules, laws or standards.
examples: The building is fully *compliant* with the fire code.
All our products are FDA-*compliant*.

senses.gloss: Too willing to do what other people want.
examples: The dictator surrounded himself with *compliant* advisers.
The medication made him quiet and more *compliant*.

senses.gloss: Having many parts or steps and hard to understand or do.
examples: The instructions are too *complicated*.
Taxes are more *complicated* than they need to be.
It's a *complicated* piece of machinery.

senses.gloss: Of a situation or relationship, difficult because of problems and mixed feelings.
examples: "Are you two together?" "It's *complicated*."
She has a *complicated* relationship with her father.

comparison: more/most — *more complimentary*; not gradable in sense 2
contrast: *Complimentary* (with *i*) means praising or free; *complementary* (with *e*) means completing each other. Same pronunciation.

senses.gloss: Saying something nice about someone or something.
examples: The reviews were very *complimentary*.
She was more *complimentary* about my cooking than I expected.

senses.gloss: Given free, especially by a hotel, restaurant or business.
examples: The hotel offers a *complimentary* breakfast.
We got two *complimentary* tickets to the game.

contrast: *Be composed of* (состоять из) is a passive verb, not this adjective: *The team is composed of ten players*.

senses.gloss: Calm and in control of your feelings.
examples: She looked *composed* during the press conference.
He took a deep breath and tried to stay *composed*.
The younger player was more *composed* under pressure.

senses.gloss: Made of different parts or materials put together.
examples: Police released a *composite* sketch of the suspect.
The deck is built from *composite* boards, not wood.
The final picture is *composite*, made from five photos.

contrast: The verb *compound* (усугублять) is stressed kuhm-POWND: *The delay compounded the problem*. The noun *a compound* is a chemical compound or a fenced group of buildings.

senses.gloss: Made of two or more parts or elements.
examples: "Toothbrush" is a *compound* word.
Flies have *compound* eyes.
He suffered a *compound* fracture of the leg.

senses.gloss: Pressed into a smaller space or size.
examples: The tires are filled with *compressed* air.
Send the photos as a *compressed* file.

senses.gloss: Shortened so that it takes less time.
examples: We're working on a *compressed* schedule this year.
The whole story is *compressed* into ninety minutes.

contrast: It does not mean "ready to compromise" — that is *willing to compromise* or *flexible*. The opposite-looking *uncompromising* does mean refusing to compromise.

senses.gloss: Showing that someone did something embarrassing, secret or wrong.
examples: The tabloid published *compromising* photos of the senator.
He was caught in a *compromising* position.
The emails were even more *compromising* than we thought.

senses.gloss: Relating to computing or calculation, especially by computers.
examples: She has a PhD in *computational* biology.
Training the model takes huge *computational* power.
The method reduces *computational* costs.

senses.gloss: Curved inward, like the inside of a bowl.
examples: A *concave* mirror makes things look bigger.
The lens is slightly *concave*.
The newer design has a more *concave* shape.

senses.gloss: Hidden from view.
examples: He has a permit to carry a *concealed* weapon.
The lights are *concealed* under the cabinets.
A *concealed* camera recorded the break-in.

senses.gloss: Thinking too highly of yourself.
examples: He's talented but so *conceited*.
I don't want to sound *conceited*, but I was right.
She's the most *conceited* person I've ever met.

senses.gloss: Possible to imagine or believe.
examples: We tried every *conceivable* solution.
It's *conceivable* that the test was wrong.
I can't think of any *conceivable* reason for the delay.

senses.gloss: Made stronger by removing water.
examples: Mix the *concentrated* juice with three cans of water.
This detergent is more *concentrated*, so use less.

senses.gloss: Directed with a lot of effort at one aim.
examples: It took a *concentrated* effort to finish on time.
The city faced a *concentrated* attack from the air.

senses.gloss: Gathered together in one place.
examples: Most of the population is *concentrated* in the cities.
Wealth is *concentrated* in a few hands.

senses.gloss: Of circles, having the same center.
examples: The stone made *concentric* ripples in the pond.
A target is a set of *concentric* circles.
The rings in a tree trunk are roughly *concentric*.

senses.gloss: Relating to ideas and concepts rather than real objects or details.
examples: The design is still at the *conceptual* stage.
The museum has a room of *conceptual* art.
Our disagreement is *conceptual*, not practical.

senses.gloss: Done with real effort and determination, often by several people together.
examples: We made a *concerted* effort to cut costs.
The two countries launched a *concerted* campaign against smuggling.
It will take *concerted* action from every state.

senses.gloss: Meant to end an argument or make someone less angry.
examples: The president struck a *conciliatory* tone in his speech.
After the fight, she sent a *conciliatory* text.
The union has become more *conciliatory* in recent talks.

senses.gloss: Giving the needed information in few words.
examples: Keep your answers clear and *concise*.
She wrote a *concise* summary of the report.
Can you make the email a little more *concise*?

senses.gloss: Coming at the end of something.
examples: Let me make a few *concluding* remarks.
The *concluding* chapter ties the story together.
Your essay needs a stronger *concluding* paragraph.

senses.gloss: Proving something so that there is no doubt.
examples: There's no *conclusive* evidence that the drug works.
The DNA results were *conclusive*.
The second study was more *conclusive* than the first.

senses.gloss: Happening at the same time as something else and connected with it; formal.
examples: Rapid growth brought *concomitant* problems like traffic.
Higher pay comes with *concomitant* responsibilities.
The risks are *concomitant* with the rewards.

contrast: Not Russian *конкурентный* (competitive) — that is *competitive*. *Concurrent* means at the same time.

senses.gloss: Happening or existing at the same time.
examples: He's serving two *concurrent* ten-year sentences.
The festival has three *concurrent* stages.
The layoffs were *concurrent* with record profits.

senses.gloss: Agreeing; in law, agreeing with a court's decision but for different reasons.
examples: Justice Kagan wrote a *concurring* opinion.
Two *concurring* judges added their own reasons.
The report cites several *concurring* expert views.

contrast: Russian *снисходительный* can be kind (lenient); English *condescending* is always negative — treating someone as less intelligent. For lenient, say *lenient* or *forgiving*.

senses.gloss: Treating people as if they are less smart or less important than you.
examples: Don't be so *condescending* to the new guys.
He explained it in a *condescending* tone.
Her second email was even more *condescending*.

senses.gloss: Depending on something else being done or happening first.
examples: The job offer is *conditional* on a background check.
They gave us *conditional* approval for the loan.

senses.gloss: In grammar, expressing a condition, usually with *if*.
examples: "If it rains, we'll stay home" is a *conditional* sentence.
We studied the *conditional* mood in Spanish class.

senses.gloss: Of a response, learned through training or repeated experience.
examples: Salivating at a bell is a *conditioned* reflex.
Fear of dentists can be a *conditioned* response.

senses.gloss: Trained or used to behaving in a certain way.
examples: We've been *conditioned* to check our phones constantly.
The dogs are *conditioned* to wait for the whistle.

position: both — mostly after a verb with *to*
contrast: Do not confuse with *conductive* (проводящий), which is about electricity and heat.

senses.gloss: Making it easier for something to happen.
examples: A noisy office isn't *conducive* to concentration.
The weather was *conducive* to a day at the beach.
Soft lighting is more *conducive* to sleep.

contrast: Do not confuse with *conducive* (способствующий): *conducive to learning*, but *conductive metal*.

senses.gloss: Able to carry electricity or heat.
examples: Copper is highly *conductive*.
Silver is even more *conductive* than copper.
The screen has a *conductive* coating.

contrast: With a capital C it refers to the Southern states that left the US in 1861. Lowercase *a confederate* is a noun — an accomplice (сообщник); the verb *confederate* ends in -rayt.

senses.gloss: Relating to the Confederacy, the Southern states that fought the North in the US Civil War.
examples: Several cities removed *Confederate* statues.
His ancestor was a *Confederate* soldier.
Richmond was the *Confederate* capital.

contrast: A false friend: *confident* is уверенный, not *конфиденциальный* — that is *confidential*. *A confidant* (with *a*) is a noun: a person you tell secrets to.

senses.gloss: Believing in your own abilities.
examples: She's a *confident* speaker.
He feels more *confident* behind the wheel now.

senses.gloss: Sure that something will happen or is true.
examples: I'm *confident* that we'll win.
The team is *confident* of a good result.
Are you *confident* about your answer?

contrast: Russian *конфиденциальный* is *confidential*, not *confident* (уверенный).

senses.gloss: Meant to be kept secret.
examples: Your answers will be kept strictly *confidential*.
He leaked *confidential* documents to the press.

senses.gloss: Of a voice or manner, showing that you are telling a secret.
examples: She lowered her voice to a *confidential* whisper.
He leaned in with a *confidential* smile.

senses.gloss: Of a space, small and enclosed.
examples: Don't run the generator in a *confined* space.
The cabin felt even more *confined* with four people.

senses.gloss: Existing only in a certain place, group or time.
examples: The damage was *confined* to the kitchen.
The problem isn't *confined* to big cities.

senses.gloss: Forced to stay in a place.
examples: She was *confined* to bed for a week with the flu.
He has been *confined* to a wheelchair since the accident.

senses.gloss: Limiting your freedom to move or act.
examples: He found office life too *confining*.
The dress was pretty but *confining*.
Small-town life felt more *confining* as she got older.
